final_answer:
SHORT ANSWER. Yes, but the I-130/I-485 denials cannot be fixed directly; the first step is the immigration court. The husband should file a motion to reopen and rescind the August 1, 2025 in absentia order based on lack of notice. If it is granted, the case can proceed to relief (renewed adjustment, subject to the I-130 problem below).

1. WHAT TO FILE WITH THE IMMIGRATION COURT (as of April 1, 2026). A written motion to reopen to rescind the in absentia order and terminate/reset proceedings, under INA 240(b)(5)(C)(ii) (8 U.S.C. 1229a(b)(5)(C)(ii)) and 8 CFR 1003.23(b)(4)(ii), arguing he did not receive notice in accordance with INA 239(a)(1) or (2). Under the statute a lack-of-notice motion may be filed at any time, so the 8-month gap is not a bar. Include a sworn declaration (when he lived where, that the mailing address was never provided by him, that he received no NTA, hearing notice, or order), evidence of his actual address (the I-130/I-485 filings and receipts, lease, mail), proof that USCIS itself used an address he never gave (the RFE and denial notices), a request to stay removal, and the applicable cover page/proof of service on DHS. Filing the motion automatically stays removal pending decision (statutory stay under 240(b)(5)(C)). He should also file Form EOIR-33 if his address is not already of record, and an EOIR-28 if represented. Presumption of delivery for regular mail is weaker than for certified mail and can be rebutted by affidavits and circumstantial evidence (Matter of M-R-A-, 24 I&N Dec. 665 (BIA 2008)). Do not rely on the alternative ground (exceptional circumstances): that must be filed within 180 days of the order, which ran about January 28, 2026, and has passed.

Key risks. (a) Under Campos-Chaves v. Garland, 602 U.S. 447 (2024), rescission requires showing he did not receive notice for the hearing he missed; if DHS or the court later mailed a hearing notice to an address he actually provided, the motion may fail. We do not know where the hearing notice was sent; the file (ROP/ECAS) should be obtained. (b) INA 239(a)(2)(B)/(c) and the address-duty rule: historically, an in absentia order could not be based on mailed notice unless the respondent was charged with receiving the NTA warnings about address obligations (Matter of G-Y-R-, 23 I&N Dec. 181 (BIA 2001)); that was good law on April 1, 2026, but I found that the BIA overruled G-Y-R- in Matter of Diji, 30 I&N Dec. 1 (BIA 2026), reported as decided September 3, 2026 (after the as-of date, found only through secondary summaries; I could not open the opinion). Diji lets DHS rely on the most recent address the person actually provided, including one given before the NTA. It should not help DHS where the mailing address was never provided by the respondent, but if he gave USCIS a different valid address on the I-130/I-485, DHS may argue that address was the one to use and was not what was mailed; this strengthens, not weakens, his argument, though it needs to be briefed.

Fee. No fee. A motion to reopen to rescind an in absentia order filed under INA 240(b)(5)(C)(ii) on lack of notice is exempt from EOIR fees (8 CFR 1003.24(b)(2)); the OBBBA (H.R. 1) fee also does not apply to such a motion, per secondary summaries. By contrast, an ordinary motion to reopen before an IJ costs $920 OBBBA + $145 INA 286(m) = $1,065 in FY2026 (rising to $1,095 on October 1, 2026), paid through the EOIR payment portal (EOIR no longer accepts checks or money orders since February 23, 2026). If the court declines to treat the motion as lack-of-notice, a fee-based fallback or a request that the IJ reopen sua sponte under 8 CFR 1003.23(b)(1) (no deadline, discretionary, extraordinary) is possible.

2. THE I-130 AND I-485 DENIALS. (a) I-130: the December 5, 2023 denial for failure to respond to the RFE is an abandonment-type denial. Under 8 CFR 103.2(b)(15), a denial due to abandonment may not be appealed, but the petitioner may file a motion to reopen under 8 CFR 103.5 (Form I-290B, fee $800 per secondary sources). The motion is due within 30 days (33 if mailed), but the deadline can be excused if the delay was reasonable and beyond the petitioner's control (8 CFR 103.5(a)(1)(i)); non-receipt due to USCIS's mailing to an address the couple never gave is a strong excuse, though a 2+ year delay will be scrutinized, and the petitioner (the wife) must file. Alternatively ask USCIS to reopen sua sponte to correct its own error (8 CFR 103.5(a)(5)), or file a new I-130 (she remains a USC and the marriage persists; new filing fee). Prepare to answer the original RFE. (b) I-485: a USCIS denial of adjustment cannot be appealed, but the applicant may renew the application before the immigration judge in removal proceedings (8 CFR 1245.2(a)(5)(ii)), and the IJ has exclusive jurisdiction over adjustment once he is in proceedings (8 CFR 1245.2(a)(1)). Once the order is rescinded and proceedings reopened, he can renew his I-485 before the IJ. Because he was inspected and admitted on a B-2 visa and is an immediate relative of a U.S. citizen, his overstay and unauthorized-status issues are not a bar to INA 245(a) adjustment (INA 245(c) exempts immediate relatives). An approved (or at least prima facie approvable and pending) I-130 is needed: the IJ cannot adjudicate the I-130, so the court may continue the case for USCIS to adjudicate it using the Matter of Hashmi, 24 I&N Dec. 785 (BIA 2009) factors. The adjustment fee for a renewed I-485 and any new I-130 are USCIS/EOIR fees I could not verify within budget.

3. SUBSTANTIVE RISK. He married 19 days after entering on a B-2; DHS may question preconceived intent / willful misrepresentation (INA 212(a)(6)(C)(i); the State Department's 90-day rule is not binding on USCIS but the facts invite scrutiny). He must prove a bona fide marriage with strong evidence. I did not verify authority on this point in this run.

4. PARALLEL STEPS. Obtain the court record, USCIS file (FOIA), and any NTA/hearing notices; update his address with USCIS (AR-11) and EOIR; avoid travel (departure after an order may be treated as self-execution of removal); consult counsel promptly because ICE can execute the order until the motion is filed.
